notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on 1 Chronicles 21, drawn from the available sources.

---

## Overview and Purpose of the Chapter

**Ellicott** notes that in 2 Samuel the census narrative is an appendix to David’s history, but here it introduces the account of preparations for building the Temple. The deviations from Samuel are more numerous than usual and reflect the Chronicler’s special purpose — showing how the Temple site was divinely chosen. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Precept Austin** (citing John Sailhamer) explains that chapter 21 fulfills the second part of God’s promise in 1 Chronicles 17:9 — “I will appoint a place for My people Israel” — meaning not merely a land but the place where God Himself would dwell, the Temple. 【https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-21-commentary】

**Guzik (Enduring Word)** notes the Chronicler passes over a large gap in David’s history (family problems, civil war) because “little of what transpired during those two decades would encourage a postexilic Judah.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 1 — “Then Satan rose up against Israel and incited David to take a census…”

### Who incited David — God or Satan?

This is the central interpretive question of the chapter, because 2 Samuel 24:1 says “the anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and He incited David,” while 1 Chronicles 21:1 names Satan.

**Traditional / Evangelical harmonisation:** Most conservative commentators hold that both statements are true at different levels. **Guzik** writes: “Satan moved David yet the LORD expressly allowed it as a chastisement against David.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】 **Precept Austin** (citing Gleason Archer) explains that “God incited him in order to teach him and his people a lesson…Satan incited him in order to deal a severe blow to Israel.” 【https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-21-commentary】

**Ellicott** takes a more nuanced linguistic approach: the Hebrew word *satan* here lacks the definite article, so it may simply mean “an adversary” (a hostile influence) rather than the personal Devil. He adds that “the adversary of our text, the influence hostile to Israel, was the wrath of God.” God did not interpose but allowed David’s corrupt motive to work out its own penal results. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Poole** (1660s): “Satan stood up, Heb. stood, to wit, before the Lord and his tribunal to accuse David and Israel, and to beg God’s permission to tempt David.” This agrees with 2 Samuel 24:1, where “the Lord is said to move David, i.e. to give Satan commission or permission to move him; for otherwise God tempteth no man, James 1:13.” 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-21.html】

### Denominational differences on v. 1

- **Reformed / Calvinist (Ligonier):** God “ordained this sin but He did so without committing sin Himself. Only David and Satan were blameworthy.” The devil is “God’s devil” — he can only colour within the lines drawn by the Almighty. Both God and Satan were involved “at different levels.” God uses even sin to accomplish His holy purposes, as with Joseph’s brothers (Gen 50:20). 【https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/davids-census】

- **Arminian / Wesleyan (Wesley’s Notes, 1765):** “Satan stood — Before the Lord and his tribunal to accuse David and Israel, and to beg God’s permission to tempt.” The emphasis falls on divine *permission*, not divine *ordination*. 【https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/21-1.html】 (The StudyLight page collates Wesley's Notes among 46 commentators.)

- **Catholic (Haydock):** “This shews that the Lord only permitted David’s sin” and in that sense only is said to have instigated him. 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/1-chronicles-21.html】

- **Modern scholarship (NET Bible note, cited on StudyLight):** “The version of the incident in the Book of 2 Samuel gives an underlying theological perspective, while the Chronicler simply describes what happened from a human perspective.” 【https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/21-1.html】

- **Desiring God (Baptist/Reformed):** Uses the concept of “secondary causation” and the divine council: “Although Satan and other members of the divine council are genuine agents…nevertheless, none of their activities is ultimately independent of God’s providence and his divine decree.” 【https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/the-divine-council】

### Other details on v. 1

**Guzik** notes this is “the first time in Scripture, the word ‘Satan’ appears without the definite article as a proper noun.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Precept Austin** speculates that Satan appealed to David’s pride — “the boastful pride of life” (1 John 2:16) — perhaps with thoughts like “Look how big your army is!” 【https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-21-commentary】

---

## v. 2 — “Go and count the Israelites from Beersheba to Dan…”

**Guzik:** The census was dangerous because of Exodus 30:12 — when Israel was counted, each man was to give a ransom “that there may be no plague among them.” In ancient Near Eastern thinking, a ruler only had the right to count what belonged to him. Israel belonged to God, not David. “It was up to the LORD to command a counting.” Citing G. Campbell Morgan: “Numbering the hosts of Jehovah is not essentially or necessarily wrong; everything depends on the motive…When it is born of pride, it is the subtlest of perils.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** The fact that Joab and the commanders were deputed “seems to prove that it was of a military character.” Also notes that the Chronicler reverses the usual “Dan to Beersheba” to “Beersheba to Dan” (south to north), reflecting his Judah-centric interests. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Expositor’s Bible Commentary** (cited on StudyLight): The Chronicler “carefully guarded against any mistake by altering ‘Dan to Beersheba’ into ‘Beersheba to Dan’” because his interests all centred in Judah. 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/1-chronicles-21.html】

---

## v. 3 — Joab’s objection

**Guzik:** Joab was not afraid to speak when the king was wrong. He “tactfully asked David to reconsider.” The hint is that David desired the increase of the nation and wanted to measure his army’s strength — “curiosity and creature-confidence” (Trapp). Late in his reign, David was tempted “to take some of the glory for himself.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** “Why will he be a cause of trespass to Israel?” is an explanatory addition by the Chronicler not found in Samuel. It makes Joab’s objection more explicit. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Poole:** “Why should this be…an occasion of punishment…to or against Israel? Why wilt thou provoke God by this sin to punish Israel? Thus he speaks, because God commonly punisheth the people for the sins of their rulers.” 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-21.html】

---

## v. 4 — “Nevertheless, the king’s word prevailed against Joab…”

**Guzik:** 2 Samuel 24:4 reveals that it wasn’t only Joab — the captains of the army also warned David. The census took nearly 10 months (2 Sam 24:5-9); David should have called it off but didn’t. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** The census belonged to the later years of David’s reign, a time of settled peace, since Joab and his chief officers had leisure for a ten-month project. The Chronicler omits the detailed route description found in 2 Samuel 24:4-8 (through Transjordan, Dan, Sidon, etc.). 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 5 — The numbers: 1,100,000 Israel, 470,000 Judah

This is one of the clearest discrepancies with 2 Samuel 24:9, which gives 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah.

**Ellicott:** The Judah figure (470,000 vs. 500,000) may be a round number in Samuel with the more exact total here. For Israel, “we may assume that the 1,100,000 of our text is an error of transcription, or, more probably, that the traditions respecting this census varied.” Alternatively, Chronicles may include David’s standing army of 288,000 men (1 Chronicles 27:1-15): 800,000 + 300,000 ≈ 1,100,000. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Pulpit Commentary:** “No really satisfactory explanation of these discrepancies has yet appeared.” It notes the “ingenious suggestion” that the Chronicler counted in the standing army for Israel and omitted a supposed 30,000 from Judah, but this “can scarcely pass muster.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/21-5.htm】

**Guzik** (citing Clarke): “To attempt to reconcile them in every part is lost labour; better at once acknowledge what cannot be successfully denied, that although the original writers of the Old Testament wrote under the influence of the Divine Spirit, yet we are not told that the same influence descended on all copiers of their words.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Guzik** also estimates total population at about 6 million based on 1,300,000 fighting men. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 6 — Levi and Benjamin not counted

**Ellicott:** Levi would naturally be exempt from a military census (Num 1:47-49). Benjamin may have been omitted because it was to be counted last (along with Judah), and Joab stopped before completing it. Josephus says Joab simply hadn’t time to include Benjamin. He may also have “feared to give offence to the tribe of Saul.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Guzik** (citing Clarke’s rabbinic explanation): Joab, seeing this would bring destruction, purposed to save two tribes. If David asked about Levi, Joab would say Levites aren’t reckoned among the children of Israel; if asked about Benjamin, he would say Benjamin had been punished enough already. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 7 — “This command was also evil in the sight of God; so He struck Israel.”

**Ellicott:** This verse is not in Samuel, which instead says “David’s heart smote him.” The Chronicler’s verse “is a sort of general heading, or anticipative summary, to the following narrative.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Guzik:** God struck Israel both by convicting David’s heart and through the coming plague. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 8 — David’s confession: “I have sinned greatly…”

**Guzik:** “The man after God’s heart was not sinless, but he had a heart sensitive to sin when he did commit it. David kept a short account with God.” Citing Morgan: “His sins were the lapses and accidents of his life…the deepest truth concerning him is revealed, not by the failures, but by his action afterwards.” David now saw “the pride and vainglory that prompted him.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** This verse is “verbatim the same with its parallel” except the characteristic substitution of “God” for “Jehovah.” David’s conscience misgave him in the night, before his interview with Gad (from 2 Samuel 24:10-11). 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## vv. 9–10 — The LORD instructs Gad the seer

**Ellicott:** Samuel says, “David arose in the morning. Now a word of Jehovah had come to Gad the prophet, a seer of David” — which Ellicott considers “more original than our text.” Gad was a long-time prophetic advisor to David (1 Sam 22:5; 1 Chron 29:29). 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Guzik:** God used David’s sin and chastisement to reveal David’s heart and wisdom. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## vv. 11–12 — Three options: famine, sword, or plague

**Guzik** unpacks the nature of each choice:
- **Three years of famine:** the wealthy and resourceful would survive; Israel would depend on neighbours.
- **Three months of defeat:** mostly soldiers would die.
- **Three days of plague:** anyone could be struck — rich or poor, royal or common. Citing Trapp: “This was a great mercy: David must be whipped; but he may choose his own rod.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** “Three years” is probably correct over Samuel’s “seven” (which may reflect a scribe’s memory of Genesis 41:30). He notes the three judgments match ancient Near Eastern curse formulas (citing the Annals of Tiglath Pileser I, c. 1120 BC, which lists overthrow of army, dwelling before foes, and pestilence). The reference to “the angel of the LORD” anticipates verse 16. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 13 — “Let me fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are very great…”

**Guzik:** David chose the plague. In famine, his wealth would protect him; in war, an ordinance already prevented him from battle (citing Clarke). But pestilence exposed him equally with the meanest subject. “David knew that God is far more merciful and gracious than man is.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** “David confesses inability to choose. So much only is clear to him, that it is better to be dependent on the compassion of God than of man.” He thus implicitly decides against the second option (military defeat), “leaving the rest to God.” Pestilence was regarded as especially divine because of “the apparent suddenness of its outbreak and the mysterious nature of its operation.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Precept Austin** notes this verse is “the thematic statement of the narrative” — the Temple site becomes the place where sinful man meets a righteous God who shows that “His mercies are very great.” 【https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-21-commentary】

---

## v. 14 — 70,000 die

**Ellicott:** From Samuel we learn the plague raged “from dawn to the time of the evening sacrifice.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Guzik:** This was a devastating calamity in such a short time. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 15 — God relents; the angel at Ornan’s threshing floor

**Guzik:** God’s relenting “justified David’s wisdom in leaving himself in God’s hands. He could not trust man to relent from destruction.” The threshing floor of Ornan is identified in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as Mount Moriah — “the same hill where Abraham offered Isaac (Genesis 22:2), and the same set of hills where Jesus died on the cross (Genesis 22:14).” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** The words “as he was destroying, the LORD beheld” are not in Samuel and “soften the harshness of the transition from the command to the countermand.” The angel was “on the point of beginning the work of death” in Jerusalem; it does not appear the city was actually touched. The spelling “Ornan” vs. Samuel’s “Araunah” reflects natural variations in spelling foreign names. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 16 — David sees the angel; he and the elders fall in sackcloth

**Ellicott:** This verse is not in Samuel, though Samuel does mention David saw the angel. “There is nothing in the style to suggest suspicion of a later hand.” The elders are mentioned here for the first time; wherever the king went, a retinue of nobles would accompany him. The drawn sword stretched out recalls Numbers 22:23 (Balaam’s angel) and Isaiah’s imagery of divine wrath (Isa 5:25; 9:12). Sackcloth was “the garb of mourners and penitents.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Guzik:** God had relented from the severity but the threat was still imminent. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 17 — David’s intercession: “These sheep, what have they done?”

**Guzik:** “Like a true shepherd, David asked that the punishment be upon him and his own household. Having another purpose to accomplish, God did not accept David’s offer.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** “These sheep” — the king as shepherd. Notes that “Is it not I that commanded…?” is “wanting” in Samuel and may have been added by the Chronicler for clarity. The final clause about “not on thy people, that they should be plagued” may comprise glosses that crept into the text. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 18 — The angel instructs Gad: build an altar at Ornan’s threshing floor

**Guzik:** This is where David met the Angel of the LORD and where God relented. Now God wanted David to meet Him there in worship. Citing Selman: “David’s altar was the only one in pre-exilic times which God explicitly commanded to be built.” Threshing floors “were usually on a height, in order to catch every breeze; some area to the north of David’s city is indicated” (Baldwin). 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** In Samuel, Gad came directly; the Chronicler introduces the angel as intermediary — a feature “only in the later prophetical books” (Daniel, Zechariah) though with precedents in Judges and Genesis. 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 19 — David goes up at Gad’s word

**Ellicott:** The variation from Samuel (“at the saying” vs. “according to”) is merely the difference “of the ‘one tittle,’ or small projection, of a letter, mentioned in Matthew 5:18.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 20 — Ornan threshing wheat; his sons hide

**Guzik** (citing Poole): The sons hid “partly because of the glory and majesty in which the angel appeared, which men’s weak and sinful natures are not able to bear; and partly for the fear of God’s vengeance, which was at this time riding circuit in the land.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott** thinks the Hebrew text here is probably corrupt: Samuel reads “Araunah looked up, and saw the king and his servants,” while Chronicles reads “saw the angel” — the Hebrew words for “angel” and “king” being similar enough to be confused in a damaged manuscript. The LXX here has “saw the king.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## vv. 21–22 — David asks to buy the threshing floor at full price

**Guzik:** David wanted to transform “this place where chaff was separated from wheat into a place of sacrifice and worship.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Ellicott:** The insistence on full price echoes Genesis 23:9 — Abraham’s purchase of the Cave of Machpelah. “The recollection of that narrative may have caused the modification of the present.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/1_chronicles/21.htm】

---

## v. 23 — Ornan’s generous offer

**Guzik:** “Ornan had a good, generous heart and wanted to give David anything he wanted.” But citing Clarke: “Had Araunah’s noble offer been accepted, it would have been Araunah’s sacrifice, not David’s; nor would it have answered the end of turning away the displeasure of the Most High.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 24 — “I will not offer burnt offerings that cost me nothing.”

**Guzik** (citing Clarke): “He who has a religion that costs him nothing, has a religion that is worth nothing: nor will any man esteem the ordinances of God, if those ordinances cost him nothing.” Also citing F.B. Meyer: “Where there is true, strong love to Jesus, it will cost us something. Love is the costliest of all undertakings…You cannot give up for Him without regaining everything you have renounced, but purified and transfigured.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## v. 25 — David pays 600 shekels of gold

**Guzik** (citing Payne): “David bought ‘the site’ — *hammaqom*, which may have included the whole area of Mount Moriah — for 240 ounces of gold. This was worth about one hundred thousand dollars. Second Samuel 24:24 notes a much smaller amount, 20 ounces of silver, for the threshing floor itself.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Kretzmann (Lutheran):** 600 shekels of gold by weight (almost $6,000 in his era), paying 50 shekels of silver for the cattle and threshing-sledge alone per 2 Samuel 24:24. 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-21.html】

---

## v. 26 — The altar built; fire from heaven

**Guzik:** Burnt offerings atoned for sin; peace offerings restored fellowship. “David understood that the death of the 70,000 in Israel in the plague did not atone for his and Israel’s sin. Atonement could only be made through the blood of an approved substitute.” Citing Spurgeon: “Abraham taught the fact of the sacrifice, while to David the reason of that sacrifice of Christ was explained. He was sacrificed to stay the plague — the plague of sin, the punishment of our iniquities.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Guzik** also notes that the fire from heaven confirmed Gad’s word that this was the place for the temple. God used Satan’s provocation to answer the question David had long pursued — where to build the temple (Psalm 132:1-5). 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Poole:** “Fire from heaven…was the sign of God’s acceptance. See Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:24, 38; 2 Chronicles 7:1.” 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mpc/1-chronicles-21.html】

**Kretzmann (Lutheran):** The offerings were “both in atonement for his sin and to restore the proper fellowship with the Lord.” Adds: “The believers of the New Testament have a better sacrifice of atonement than that of David; for the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, cleanses us from all sins.” 【https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-21.html】

---

## v. 27 — The angel sheathes his sword

**Guzik:** The LORD commanded the angel, who returned his sword to its sheath. God’s acceptance of the sacrifice brought the plague to an end. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## vv. 28–30 — David sacrifices there; the tabernacle at Gibeon; David’s fear

**Guzik:** David knew God had sanctified the place Himself with fire. “Having seen his prayers answered and his sacrifices accepted, the site had already become a ‘house of prayer’ and a ‘temple for sacrifices’” (Selman). The tabernacle and altar were at Gibeon, but David couldn’t go there — he was afraid of the angel’s sword. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

**Gill:** David “was so weak that he could not go; and he feared that, should he attempt to go, while he was going thither, at such a distance, the angel would make a terrible slaughter in Jerusalem…and besides, as the Lord had commanded him to build an altar there, he might fear it would displease him, should he depart from it.” 【https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_chronicles/21.htm】

**Guzik** (citing Spurgeon): “Do not believe for a moment that visible grandeur is necessary to the place where God will meet with you. Go to your threshing floor and pray…Fear not to draw nigh to God in these streets, but consecrate all space to the Lord your God.” 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## Chapter Conclusion (22:1) — “This is the house of the LORD God”

**Guzik:** David understood the future temple should be built on this spot. Citing Trapp: “This is that very place foretold by Moses (Deuteronomy 12:11).” Guzik then draws spiritual lessons from the character of Ornan’s threshing floor: it was a simple, unadorned place; a place of ordinary work; a place bought with money; a place from which bread came; a place where God’s justice was evident; where sin was confessed; and where sacrifice was offered and accepted. 【https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-21/】

---

## Summary of Denominational Distinctives

| Tradition | Key Emphasis on This Chapter |
|---|---|
| **Reformed** (Ligonier, Desiring God) | God sovereignly ordained the sin without committing it; Satan was a secondary agent. God uses evil for greater good — here, revealing the Temple site. |
| **Arminian/Wesleyan** (Wesley’s Notes) | Satan acted with God’s *permission*, not ordination. Emphasis on Satan as accuser before God’s tribunal. |
| **Catholic** (Haydock) | God “only permitted” David’s sin; no suggestion of divine ordination. The census was sinful because it was motivated by pride, not by God’s command. |
| **Lutheran** (Kretzmann) | Reads Ornan’s bowing to David through the lens of the Fourth Commandment. Emphasises that David’s sacrifice points forward to Christ’s better atonement. |
| **Baptist/Evangelical** (Spurgeon, Guzik) | Strong Christological reading of the threshing floor as foreshadowing Calvary. Emphasis on personal application: costly sacrifice, true repentance, short accounts with God. |
| **Modern Scholarship** (NET Bible note, Ellicott) | The Chronicler gave a “human perspective” (Satan), while 2 Samuel gave the “theological perspective” (God). The Chronicler’s purpose was to explain how the Temple site was chosen, not merely to recount history. |
